attempts.raw_response: Later, the algorithm was refined and renamed GPSR to improve efficiency and adaptability in dynamic wireless environments. By switching between local greedy forwarding and perimeter traversal only when necessary, GPSR minimizes overhead while maintaining robustness against node failures or irregular network topologies. This hybrid approach has become a foundational protocol for geographic routing in sensor networks, enabling scalable communication without requiring global position knowledge or complex state maintenance at each intermediate node.

Face routing depends on a planar subgraph in general; however distributed planarization is difficult for real wireless sensor networks and does not scale well to 3D environments.

Greedy embedding
Although originally developed as a routing scheme that uses the physical positions of each node, geographic routing algorithms have also been applied to networks in which each node is associated with a point in a virtual space, unrelated to its physical position. The process of finding a set of virtual positions for the nodes of a network such that geographic routing using these positions is guaranteed to succeed is called greedy embedding.
pair.prefix: Then, face routing helps to recover from that situation and find a path to another node, where greedy forwarding can be resumed. A recovery strategy such as face routing is necessary to assure that a message can be delivered to the destination. The combination of greedy forwarding and face routing was first proposed in 1999 under the name GFG (Greedy-Face-Greedy). It guarantees delivery in the so-called unit disk graph network model.
